questions.question: A speedometer shows 60 km/h at one instant. How does that number relate to an average speed over a journey?
questions.solution: Average speed = total distance/total time (a secant slope). The speedometer is the LIMIT of average speeds as the interval shrinks to zero — the tangent slope, f′(t). The derivative is defined as lim(h→0)[f(t+h) − f(t)]/h: an average rate taken to its limit.

questions.question: Why does d/dx(x²) = 2x, and what does the power rule do for x^(1/2)?
questions.solution: From first principles: (x+h)² − x² = 2xh + h²; dividing by h gives 2x + h → 2x as h→0. The power rule generalises: d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹ — so x^(1/2) differentiates to ½x^(−1/2), the slope of the square-root curve. One rule covers all powers, fractional or negative.

questions.question: If y = (3x + 1)², why must the chain rule be used and what does it give?
questions.solution: y is a composite: outer function u², inner u = 3x+1. Rates multiply: dy/dx = dy/du · du/dx = 2u · 3 = 6(3x+1). Forgetting the inner derivative (3) is the classic error — the chain rule accounts for the fact that u itself changes as x changes.

questions.question: How does the sign of f′(x) tell you whether a function rises or falls, and what does f′ = 0 mark?
questions.solution: f′ is the slope: positive — the curve climbs; negative — it falls. f′ = 0 marks a STATIONARY point (horizontal tangent) — a candidate for maximum, minimum or inflection (which one needs further testing). Reading the derivative's sign turns a formula into a picture of the graph.

questions.question: Why does every indefinite integral carry '+C', and why does a definite integral not need it?
questions.solution: Differentiation erases constants, so reversing it recovers a whole FAMILY of functions differing by a constant — +C stands for that family. In a definite integral the constant cancels: [F(b)+C] − [F(a)+C] = F(b) − F(a). The +C is the price of information lost by differentiation.
